webTitle: Trump’s new attorney general poses a huge threat to abortion rights | Moira Donegan

fields.headline: Trump’s new attorney general poses a huge threat to abortion rights
fields.trailText: A call revealing Todd Blanche’s plans to crack down on mifepristone lays bare the danger
fields.bodyText: The abortion pill is a miracle. Mifepristone, then called RU-486, was synthesized by a French lab in the 1980s; in combination with misoprostol, commonly used as ulcer medication, it cuts off the body’s supply of progesterone, halts the development of a pregnancy, and incites contractions, which empty the uterus. The drug allows pregnancies to be terminated with a shocking degree of reliability and ease. Gone are the concoctions of ergot and Spanish Fly dispensed by 19th century midwives, which only sometimes worked to induce a miscarriage; gone are the backroom procedures of the pre-Roe US, when drunk, lascivious, incompetent or cruel providers wielded bent coat hangers in dirty rooms. The abortion pill is safe, effective and cheaper than ever. And since Dobbs, it’s everywhere: even if you live in a state with an abortion ban, you can get the pills shipped to your house in the mail. Since Roe was overturned, there has not been a return to the terror of mass death that marked the pre-Roe era of septic abortion wards, where women routinely found themselves maimed, sickened or killed. There’s exactly one reason why: because illegal abortions were largely unsafe without the pill, and they are extremely safe with it. So of course, the Trump administration and their allies on the American right are trying to get rid of it. And this month, they gained a powerful new ally when Todd Blanche, Donald Trump’s former personal lawyer and an anti-abortion zealot, was confirmed as attorney general. The vote, in which Blanche was confirmed by a margin of one along party lines, was conducted in the wee hours of the morning on 8 August. Maybe that’s because the Republicans who confirmed him didn’t want anyone to see what they were doing. Blanche has, after all, been shockingly subservient to Donald Trump, and seems poised to complete the president’s long-brewing transformation of the country’s chief law enforcement agency into a vehicle for score settling, personal vendettas, distributing favors to the administration’s friends and suppressing dissent from its political enemies. But perhaps most incendiary is what Blanche has said, publicly and privately, about how he intends to use the justice department and its vast array of oversight powers, legal prerogatives, and investigatory purview to curtail abortion access nationwide – and to shut down the life-saving distribution of mifepristone, in particular. In a call facilitated by the White House faith office just days before he was confirmed, Blanche reportedly told Christian conservative leaders that as attorney general, he would move more aggressively than his predecessor Pam Bondi to outlaw the mailing of mifepristone across state lines, and target the Democratic-controlled states that have protected abortion most effectively. Blanche, who was then the acting AG, told the religious group Intercessors for America that the justice department was working “so that the Dobbs decision becomes permanent in every single state.” “We don’t have complete victory yet,” Blanche said, “but we will have victory, and victory will be soon, and, and, and it will be permanent.” Exactly how Blanche intends to secure his victory over women’s freedom is unclear. But as AG, he has several paths at his disposal. His comments on the call prompted widespread speculation that Blanche could call for enforcement of the Comstock Act, a long-dormant law from 1873 that has been unenforced for years and has been partially repealed in the past. Anti-choice advocates say it could be used to legally ban the mailing of abortion pills, thus cutting off access for many women who live in states with bans. In 2022, the Biden justice department declared that medical providers could not be prosecuted under the Comstock Act for mailing abortion pills; as the attorney general, Blanche would have the power to reverse that decision. The Comstock Act’s application would be particularly significant, as it could be used to halt virtually all commercial traffic in abortion pills – not only mifepristone, but also misoprostol, the second drug, which has sometimes been used to induce abortion on its own. Such a move would reverse the miracle of the pills, pushing many desperate women towards methods that are less effective and can carry grave dangers. Another path that Blanche could take to restrict abortion access would be to sue the states that seek to protect it. On the call, Blanche explained his reasoning: “If states have said, ‘We are going to protect the unborn and we’re going to protect every life from the moment of conception,’ we’re putting practices and policies in place so that other states and other organizations can’t attack that. They can’t do things like they’re doing with mailing in mail-order drugs.” Here, Blanche appeared to be referencing shield laws, legislation passed in a number of Democratic-controlled states that prohibits state authorities from participating in other states’ abortion-related investigations and prosecutions. The laws mean that doctors operating out of states like New York or Washington can prescribe and ship abortion drugs to people living in places such as Texas or Arkansas, safe in the knowledge that their own state police will not come knocking at their door to serve another state’s warrant or extradition order. Blanche’s comments suggest that his Department of Justice might sue to have the shield laws declared illegal, thus significantly curtailing liberal states’ rights to choose their own law enforcement priorities and granting conservative states the power to enforce their own laws even beyond their borders. Blanche also appeared to indicate that he would seek to restrict abortion access using other agencies’ powers. On his call with leaders of the Christian right, he said his department was “working hand in hand” with health agencies to make Dobbs permanent. The FDA, which expanded access to mifepristone in 2021 under the Biden administration and made the change permanent in 2023, has been under intense pressure from anti-choice allies in the Maga coalition to revise that guidance, making the drug ineligible for telehealth prescriptions and requiring patients to retrieve it from providers in person, a regulatory move that would also serve to cut off access in Republican controlled states. But the anti-abortion movement is pushing the FDA even further: it has succeeded in getting the agency to initiate a “review” of mifepristone’s safety (though the safety of the drug has been proven by nearly four decades of use worldwide and hundreds of studies), which is widely seen as a pathway for the FDA to create a pretext to remove mifepristone from the market. That’s not fast enough for some on the misogynist right: Louisiana has sued the FDA, asking it to forbid mifepristone from being prescribed via telehealth, in a case that is set to be heard by the ultraconservative fifth circuit next month. So far, the justice department has supported the drug’s online availability in court. Under Blanche, it could reverse that stance. Trump has been gunshy about pursuing the agenda of his antiabortion allies since returning to office. He appears to have been spooked by the political reaction to Dobbs, which was credited for the Democrats’ better-than-expected showing in the 2022 midterms, as well as with a slew of pro-choice victories in special elections in the years that immediately followed the decision. The anti-choice movement has even been angry with Trump for the slow pace of his anti-abortion agenda since his return to power in 2025. Which is not to say that the Trump administration has given the movement nothing: enforcement of the Face Act, a federal law meant to stop anti-choice protestors from physically blocking clinic entrances, has been all but abandoned since Trump returned to the White House; some who were prosecuted under the law have even been pardoned and remunerated by Trump, at taxpayer expense. But until now, Trump has faced a looming threat that seems to have slowed the pace of his anti-abortion policymaking: the 2026 midterms. Soon, that obstacle will be removed. The appointment of Todd Blanche is a dark signal for women’s rights: more abortion restrictions can be expected in 2027. Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

webTitle: Persuasion, denial and bluster: Trump ‘stuck’ on Iran war ahead of elections

fields.headline: Persuasion, denial and bluster: Trump ‘stuck’ on Iran war ahead of elections
fields.trailText: As the president tries to extract the US from his Iran war quagmire, leadership in Tehran is only too happy to crush his midterm dreams
fields.bodyText: In the aftermath of his devastating election defeat, the US president remained haunted by regrets over Iran. Months before Jimmy Carter lost the 1980 presidential election to Ronald Reagan, eight US servicemen died in a botched high-risk rescue mission that failed to secure the freedom of dozens of US hostages seized in Tehran. As he addressed students and academics, keen for reflections on his single-term presidency, one of the students asked Carter: what do you most regret? “Not sending more helicopters for the hostage rescue,” he immediately replied, according to Larry Sabato, director of the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, who hosted the former president. “It was very much on his mind,” said Sabato. Carter’s fate nearly half a century ago may also be on the mind of Donald Trump as he prepares to embark upon a midterm election campaign over the coming months, while embroiled in a military struggle with Tehran. The Iranian regime is proving equally intractable to that faced by his Democratic predecessor. Trump’s efforts to finish the war he started along with Israel almost six months ago, on 28 February, have foundered after a ceasefire agreement signed in June collapsed – leaving Iran in control of the strait of Hormuz, a waterway that was the conduit for one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies before the conflict. The Iranian stranglehold has pushed up oil prices, stoked inflation and raised living costs in the US, all as Trump’s Republican party already faced an uphill struggle to retain control of US Congress in November’s midterm elections. With public support for the war running low, polls show a majority of American voters believe they are worse off since Trump returned to office in January 2025. That indicator alone has echoes of Reagan’s famous question to voters during his 1980 presidential debate with Carter: “Are you better off than you were four years ago?” ‘Trump can’t change course’ While the circumstances are different, Trump’s troubles have a broader resemblance to Carter’s dilemma, which began when revolutionaries stormed the US embassy in November 1979 and held 52 diplomats and military personnel hostage. That was compounded after a daring rescue attempt the following April had to be aborted when three out of eight helicopters deployed on the mission developed mechanical faults. One of the remaining craft collided with a transport plane, killing eight US servicemen and intensifying the ignominy. Later efforts to negotiate the hostages’ release before the presidential election failed, most notably on the weekend before polling day, when a putative deal collapsed, making Carter’s electoral defeat almost certain. They were eventually released after 444 days in captivity, minutes after Reagan was sworn into office on 20 January 1981. The historic parallels are imprecise, but sufficient to be perceived by both Trump and Iran’s current leaders, analysts say. “Carter couldn’t change course, and maybe that’s what’s most applicable, because Trump can’t change course either,” said Sabato. “Carter was stuck because, after the failed rescue, the hostages were dispersed throughout Iran and there was no way to recover them. “Trump is stuck because he never had a good rationale [for the war]. He just wanted another victory. All they had to say to Trump to get him to go in was ‘Mr President, this is just going to be another Venezuela, and then we can go in and do Cuba.’” With a 60-day ceasefire since June’s memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June lapsing this week without any formal resolution, Trump now faces entering an election campaign on the back of an unpopular war that he appears to be losing. Payback time? So far, Trump has responded with a mixture of half-hearted persuasion, denial and threatening bluster. Appearing at the Nassau county police academy in Garden City, New York, on 14 August, he downplayed the war’s impact on fuel prices as necessary to prevent “an evil country” obtaining a nuclear weapon. “Remember that, when you have to pay a little bit more, you’re at $4, it’s OK,” he said. In an interview with Fox News, he then threatened to “bomb the shit out of” Oman if it “gets in the way” of efforts to end the conflict with Iran. In a futile gesture that drew Iranian mockery, he also declared the strait of Hormuz a “new US territory” on social media. And in recent days, the president has threatened to unleash “Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale” against Iran – omitting details of what precisely this might mean, but vaguely warning countries that provide “any type of lifeline” to Tehran that they, too, will suffer. The fluctuations seem to betray frustration over a paucity of viable options – a predicament that analysts expect Iran’s leaders to exploit by seeking to deepen Trump’s unpopularity as the midterms approach. “They are determined to make him pay the consequences of starting this war at the midterm elections,” said Vali Nasr, an Iran expert and international relations professor at Johns Hopkins University. The approach involves depriving Trump of the option of putting the war on the back burner, or simply declaring victory. “The whole point Iran is making is that ‘We’re not going to let him decide the sort of ebb and flow of this war,’” said Nasr. “Their position is ‘We have a vote here, and we’re not just going to make it convenient for him’ … “They have intimated that they are giving him four weeks to go back to the MOU and fully implement it, otherwise they are going to escalate. That means a broader scale of attacks on Gulf targets, more attacks on US bases and US military assets. It’s exactly the opposite of this going low-key, and off the front pages of newspapers.” The more aggressive Iranian stance has been signaled by a recent shake-up in the regime’s leadership that has included the promotion of Mohsen Rezaei, a former commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for most of the 1980-88 war with Iraq, as secretary of the powerful supreme national security council. The reshuffle also includes the appointment of Hossein Taeb, a hardline cleric and former intelligence chief, as head of the Basij, a volunteer militia, with a brief to turn it into a neighborhood surveillance unit that will root out domestic opposition and perceived Israeli penetration of Iranian society. ‘Really not in a hurry’ “It’s fair to say that the Iranians have decided that they are going to make life more miserable for Trump in a variety of ways,” said Mehrzad Boroujerdi, a political scientist and vice-provost at Missouri Science and Technology University. “They are certainly going to do whatever they can to hurt him in the midterms. “Every US public opinion poll I have seen makes a direct correlation with the Iran war and that’s in the minds of the White House in terms of what to do, and the reason we are seeing this switch from Trump threatening military action to basically resigning himself to this idea of the economy being the achilles heel of the Iranian regime, and trying to pressure them to come to the negotiating table. “But they are really not in a hurry. They do not see the economic condition as that dire for them.” What may become increasingly dire in the run-up to the midterms is the outlook for the US and global economy, according to Alan Eyre, a former state department Iran specialist, who argued that a race between “two ticking economic clocks” would favor Iran. “It’s going to get ugly as we head into the midterms,” he said. “We have buffered it to an extent by releasing oil from the strategic petroleum reserve, jawboning the market, and by the Chinese decreasing oil imports, but the resiliency of the system is decreasing significantly and an inflation spike is on the way.” The driver of a coming economic crunch, argued Eyre, is the rising price of diesel, central to the modern economy because it is the essential fuel in supply chains. “Diesel price is currently $5.44 a gallon. A week ago, $5.30 a gallon. A month ago, $5.06 a gallon. A year ago, $3.70 a gallon,” he said. Facing an array of bad options, Trump’s only recourse is to choose the least worse – which may also be tantamount to admitting defeat. “The least bad option is trying to reopen the strait of Hormuz as quickly as possible, as much as possible, under Iranian control, because they are not going to give up control of the strait in the short to mid-term,” said Eyre, who was the state department’s first Farsi-speaking spokesperson under the Obama administration at a time when it was trying to forge stronger ties with Iranian communities across the world. But Iran is not proffering Trump an olive branch in his hour of need. ‘An electoral wood chipper’? Even reopening the strait is unlikely to trigger an immediate economic revival as maritime insurance companies take time to assess whether the waterway is safe for ships to use again. Trump may be oblivious to the electoral fate of members of his own party in US Congress, whom he has treated with scant regard. “He sees his brand as separate and better than the Republican brand,” said Eyre. “And the fact that the Republican party might be walking into an electoral wood chipper in November doesn’t really seem to be motivating him.” Trump, indeed, may already be preparing for life under a Democratic-controlled Congress. This month he announced the appointment of Will Scharf, a rightwing lawyer, as the new White House legal counsel, with the apparent brief of fighting off an anticipated wave of Democratic demands for subpoenas, documents and congressional investigations. The president, who publicly refused to accept his defeat to Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election, has also been laying the groundwork to challenge the integrity of November’s poll results, too. Engineering a electoral drubbing for Trump remains a prize worth pursuing for Iran’s leaders. Such an outcome would set the stage for congressional Democrats to ramp up scrutiny of US conduct in the war. The outcome of the elections, now less than three months away, “could make the last two years of Trump’s presidency much more difficult for him, and make him much less effective”, said Nasr, of John Hopkins University. “It’s not just the midterms. The day after the elections, all focus will shift to 2028. “If Trump doesn’t have a way to finish this war, or it becomes nastier with a greater impact on the global economy, then it will begin to become an issue for the presidential election.” Even that might pale in comparison with the visceral satisfaction a now ageing revolutionary leadership generation would take in delivering a coup de grace reminiscent of that dealt to Carter 46 years ago. “Why wouldn’t they do the same thing?” asked Sabato, who recalled how Carter reacted with grim resignation when he learned that the last chance of an 11th-hour pre-election deal to free the hostages had collapsed. “They remember the history, and they won then. “They want to win again against a foe that I’m sure they despise much more than Jimmy Carter. For them, this guy is worse in every way that a human being can be worse.”

webTitle: Trump talks up White House ballroom and says he views strait of Hormuz as ‘American territory’ – as it happened

fields.headline: Trump talks up White House ballroom and says he views strait of Hormuz as ‘American territory’ – as it happened
fields.trailText: President in South Carolina celebrates supreme court’s temporary order to allow construction to continue and discusses war in Iran
fields.bodyText: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: Donald Trump thanked the supreme court for allowing work to proceed, for now, on what he has taken to calling his White House “Military/Ballroom Complex”. The president’s brief post was packed with misleading or false claims about the order and the ballroom he razed the entire East Wing of the White House to build. Trump was asked if he could “guarantee that no tax money will be used in the construction of the ballroom?” The president replied, as he has for over a year, by insisting that the project would be entirely paid for by private donations, despite multiple reports that the project will drain hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars from federal agencies. The US Postal Service prepared to publish a final ⁠rule late ⁠on Friday to impose new requirements on states to provide the federal government with information on voters ahead of the November ⁠midterm congressional elections, despite a pair of court ‌orders ‌that currently block the ‌changes from taking effect. The Pentagon fired the publisher and editor in chief of Stars and Stripes, a US military news outlet partly funded by taxpayers, as well as a reporter after the outlet drew attention to dire conditions for service members fighting Iran. Trump threatened a prominent progressive think tank, the Center for American Progress, with a $5bn lawsuit over its report that found the president’s expensive deployment of the national guard and other federal agents has done little to reduce violent crime in Washington DC and other cities. The US Postal Service prepared to publish a final ⁠rule late ⁠on Friday to impose new requirements on states to provide the federal government with information on voters ahead of the November ⁠midterm congressional elections, despite a pair of court ‌orders ‌that currently block the ‌changes from taking effect. The USPS acknowledged in the text of the final rule posted online Friday, which is scheduled to be published in the Federal Register next week, that two injunctions issued by federal courts in California and Massachusetts currently bar it from moving ahead with the changes to comply with a March executive order signed by Donald Trump. In accordance with the order, the postal service would ‌require states to give the US Department of Homeland Security and other agencies access to lists of voters and to adopt new balloting procedures before the mail agency would make deliveries. If states did not comply, USPS would refuse to deliver the ballots. The federal government has sued 30 states and Washington DC, for refusing to hand over lists of eligible voters. Despite the injunctions, the Trump administration is pressing ahead with plans to disrupt votes cast by mail. According to the text posted online Friday, the USPS is ready to implement the new restrictions on mail-in voting if the court injunctions are lifted. If the government obtains timely relief from the injunctions, implementation immediately thereafter will provide election officials as much time as possible before the next election to comply with the rule’s preparation standards for Federal Ballot Mail envelopes, and to prepare to submit data to the Federal Ballot Mail Portal (“Portal”), before the mail-in and absentee ballots subject to this rule are mailed (which generally occurs in September or thereafter, as determined by state law). The Portal will become active (along with the verification process that relies on Portal data) at the time of the publication of the system of records (“SOR”) governing the Portal. Nearly one in three Americans voted by mail in 2024, but Trump, who wants to restrict the number of voters by limiting ballots cast by mail, signed an executive order in March that prohibits the USPS from delivering ballots to any voters not on a federal list of citizens deemed eligible to vote in each state by the Department of Homeland Security. The USPS proposal to implement this order seeks to require states to give the postal service the names and barcodes tied to mail-in ballots for federal elections. The service said it received more than 200,000 responses to its proposed rule change during a public comment period. Trump himself voted by mail in Florida’s Republican primary this year, which was at least the third time the president has mailed his ballot. Trump has ended his campaign rally for Darline Graham in South Carolina after speaking for nearly 90 minutes, including joking about bombing Iran and recycling a decade-old complaint about Hillary Clinton. At one point, the president asked the crowd if they wanted to hear him recite The Snake, a poem he used to frequently reference at campaign events about a woman who takes in a snake that later bites her. He said, “Do you want to hear The Snake? Look, it’s a Friday night. We have plenty of time, right? What the hell do I have to do? Go back, bomb Iran a little bit more?” Trump also returned to an attack line against his 2016 revival, Hillary Clinton, mentioning her “deplorables” gaffe from ten years ago. In another moment, he brought up Karoline Leavitt, his press secretary who is stepping down and had a baby earlier this year. “She just had a baby, and I just learned she loves the baby more than she loves Donald Trump, and I’m very angry with her,” the president said. Trump was supporting Graham in advance of the Republican runoff on Tuesday to succeed her late brother, Lindsey. She is up against the ultra-conservative representative Ralph Norman and made headlines earlier this week when she stumbled during a debate and said, “I’m just going to be honest here. I’m not that informed on national security.” A protester wearing a “kill your local pedophile” shirt was ejected from a Trump rally in support of the South Carolina Senate campaign of Darline Graham, according to a Washington Examiner reporter at the event. The demonstrator also wore a hat with an upside down American flag. The protester briefly interrupted a speech by the president, who has been delving into familiar campaign speech subjects, railing against “communist” Democrats and repeatedly returning to attacks on transgender people. Discussing the war with Iran at a South Carolina campaign event, Trump said: “I view the strait of Hormuz as an American territory right now. It’s an American territory.” The president has faced scrutiny in recent days for making similar remarks as his administration struggles to end the war and gas prices reach record high levels. During a speech in New York last week, Trump said he would “pretty soon” designate the strait a US territory. The strait is a crucial waterway for global trade, bordered by Iran and Oman, and Tehran has refused to reopen it as peace talks continue to stall. The president also recently claimed on social media that the US had “total control” over the strait, saying, “I think we will keep it.” Last week, Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, responded that Tehran would not ⁠be intimidated by the president’s threats and that the strait of Hormuz would only be opened under Iran’s authority. Speaking at a campaign rally for Darline Graham in South Carolina, Trump is praising his poll numbers while also complaining about polls that reflect poorly on him: Except for the fake polls out there, my poll numbers are great … they have such fake polls. So we have the greatest economy in our history. Now some people haven’t seen it yet, but they will, because the job numbers are so good … We have the greatest poll numbers that I’ve ever had. We have the greatest economy that I’ve ever had.” A recent Reuters/Ipsos ‌poll found Americans preferred Democrats over Republicans as stewards of the economy for the first time in nearly a decade. That poll also found Americans’ approval of the president’s performance falling to 35%. An ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll. And a recent YouGov/Economist projection found Trump’s net job approval is negative in all but three states. The president is now speaking at a rally in support of the Senate campaign of Darline Graham, the sister of the late senator, Lindsey Graham. After a few minutes of praise for her campaign, Trump began discussing his ballroom project, saying he was in a “very good mood” after US supreme court chief justice John Roberts issued an order in his favor earlier today. The order allowed the White House to continue construction of the ballroom, a top Trump priority, while appeals challenging the project are ongoing. At the rally, Trump described the ballroom as a “beautiful, magnificent complex, being built on the hallowed grounds of our cherished White House”. He said the ballroom was “so vital for national security” and would be “the greatest of its kind anywhere that’s ever been built”. Concerns about the narrow, partisan nature of the media consumed by the president of the United States have spiked in recent days amid new attention to the role Donald Trump’s aide, Natalie Harp, plays in limiting what he sees, by printing out mainly flattering headlines and posts for him from the internet for him to read. Trump himself accidentally offered up evidence of just how skewed his media diet is on Friday, when he used a few minutes with reporters to hold up a print-out of what he cast as important media headlines before boarding a flight to South Carolina for a rally in support of the Senate campaign of late Lindsey Graham’s sister, Darline. “So, here are some headlines,” the president said after asking his press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, to hand him a print-out that displayed nine headlines, but no indiction of where they were published. “These are incredible headlines that just came out over the last 24 hours.” “It’s probably easier if I show them to you than reading them,” Trump said, holding up the sheet of paper in front of photographers in the White House pool. He then boasted about the headlines, which were largely taken from partisan, right-wing outlets that openly support him and simply repeated his administration’s claims. Two of the headlines came from Breitbart, the far-right website its former editor Steve Bannon once described as a “platform for the alt-right”. Two came from outlets owned by Trump supporter Rupert Murdoch: the New York Post and Fox News. One was an opinion piece from a former Trump campaign spokesman published by the Daily Signal, a website founded by the Heritage Foundation, the right-wing think tank behind Project 2025. One came from Voz, a conservative news site aimed at Latinos founded in 2022 by pro-Trump executives. The other three headlines came from avowedly non-partisan news outlets, Axios, CNN and the Washington Post, but in all three cases the headlines simply presented what looked like good news that the administration took credit. As we reported last week, when Trump held up the Washington Post headline “Prescription drug prices record sharpest drop in more than 60 years”, the president apparently failed to read the article below, since it reported that independent experts actually attributed the price drop to Joe Biden, not Trump. The secretary of the US Army, Dan Driscoll, is expected to step down from his role by the end of the year, after months of tension with the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday. Driscoll, a friend and Yale Law school classmate of vice-president JD Vance, reportedly angered Hegseth near the very start of his tenure at the Pentagon when he offered to set up a visit by Vance and Donald Trump. The departure, as the US is engaged in a war with Iran, would further deplete the US Army of Senate-confirmed leaders. In April, Hegseth fired the Army’s chief of staff, General Randy George and a replacement has yet to be nominated. Speaking to reporters on his way to a political rally in South Carolina, Donald Trump was asked if he could “guarantee that no tax money will be used in the construction of the ballroom?” The president replied, as he has for over a year, by insisting that the project would be entirely paid for by private donations, despite multiple reports that the project will drain hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars from federal agencies. “We’re spending hundreds of millions of dollars on the ballroom and it’s all from people like me and great companies that are putting it up. It’s going to be close to $400 million and it’s all paid for by patriots and patriotic companies,” Trump said. “No taxpayer money for the ballroom at all.” But the Washington Post reported in June that Trump’s claim is simply untrue. A project summary prepared by the ballroom contractor obtained by the Post showed that the total construction was expected to cost $600m, with more than half of the funds coming from taxpayers. Two days later, the New York Times revealed that the Trump administration had shifted over $350m from the Secret Service’s budget to White House to pay for a secure military bunker underneath the luxury ballroom. In a social media post on Friday, Donald Trump thanked the supreme court for allowing work to proceed, for now, on what he has taken to calling his White House “Military/Ballroom Complex”. The president’s brief post was packed with misleading or false claims about the order and the ballroom he razed the entire East Wing of the White House to start building. “We are grateful for the Decision of the United States Supreme Court”, Trump wrote, mischaracterizing the single-sentence order from one justice, John Roberts, as a decision of the court. In fact, Roberts only lifted a preliminary injunction from a lower court that had blocked above-ground work on the ballroom to give the full supreme court time to reach a final decision on whether the president can complete the project. “The Military/Ballroom Complex being built on the hallowed grounds of the White House, which is so vital for National Security, will be THE GREATEST OF ITS KIND!” Trump continued, continuing to cast the creation of a vast reception hall on the White House grounds as somehow motivated by a concern to increase security around the presidential residence. A White House bunker beneath the East Wing, demolished by Trump in his rush to construct his ballroom, does need to be replaced, but he is simply solving a problem he created. Trump was reportedly rushed into the bunker by the Secret Service in 2020, as protesters rallied to decry police violence against Black Americans after the murder of George Floyd. “It is something that Presidents have wanted for 150 years, and that the Military has been seeking for the last 100 years,” Trump continued, repeating an entirely unsourced claim he has been making for more than a year now. “Their wish will soon be fulfilled! Construction is under budget and ahead of schedule,” he concluded. Although this is a claim Trump has been making about building projects since his days as a real estate developer, it is clearly not true that construction of the ballroom is “under budget” given that the White House first said the ballroom would cost approximately $200m when it was unveiled in July 2025, before the president started calling if a $400m project, and the contractor hired for the ballroom reportedly told the White House in March that the project cost had soared to $600m, according to a document obtained by the Washington Post. Senator Chuck Schumer, who leads the Democratic minority in the Senate, denounced the supreme court order Trump hailed. “The MAGA Supreme Court is rubber stamping Trump’s vanity-driven, gilded corruption,” Schumer posted in response to the news. “As costs skyrocket, the administration is wasting money on an endless and illegal war, corporate giveaways, and Trump’s pet projects,” Schumer added. “We will continue to fight this flagrant waste of taxpayer money relentlessly in the courts.” In an update to my earlier post, the Pentagon is confirmed to have fired the editor-in-chief of Stars and Stripes, Erik Slavin, as well as its publisher, Max Lederer, and a reporter, Slavin has told the Associated Press. Slavin said he was dismissed for insubordination after an interview he gave that objected to any potential censorship by the US military. He told the AP he was fired “for stating in a CBS interview that hypothetical censorship of news for service members would constitute a red line”. He added that he stands by the principle “that Stars and Stripes must remain editorially independent”. Earlier this week, Lederer announced his retirement effective at the end of September. He too received a separation notice, according to Slavin, as did the Middle East reporter Lara Korte.
